meta.title: MCP Question Bank — Chapter 11 (Multi-Select): JSON-RPC 2.0 Fundamentals
meta.format: multi_select: questions use the 'answers' array (multiple correct options). Some include an 'All of the above' option that is only correct when every other option is.

questions.question: Which members can legally appear in a JSON-RPC 2.0 Request object? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: jsonrpc (must be exactly "2.0")
method (a String; names starting with 'rpc.' are reserved)
params (optional; must be an Array or Object when present)
id (String, Number, or Null; omit it to make the request a notification)
headers (an Object of transport headers)

questions.explanation: jsonrpc, method, params, and id are the four members. Transport headers live outside the JSON-RPC payload.

questions.question: Which statements about JSON-RPC 2.0 Response objects are true? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Exactly one of result or error must be present — never both
The id must equal the request's id
If the request's id couldn't be detected (parse error / invalid request), the response id must be Null
A response is returned for every notification
The error object's code must be an integer

questions.explanation: Notifications get no response by definition — the server MUST NOT reply to them, even inside batches. The other four rules are verbatim from the spec.

questions.question: Which reserved error-code facts are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: -32700 Parse error — invalid JSON received
-32601 Method not found
-32602 Invalid params
-32000 to -32099 is reserved for implementation-defined server errors
-32768 to -32000 is freely available for application-defined errors

questions.explanation: The -32768..-32000 range is RESERVED for pre-defined errors; the remainder of the space (outside it) is what's available for application-defined errors.

questions.question: Which batch-call rules does the JSON-RPC 2.0 spec state? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The server may process batch requests concurrently and in any order
Responses may return in any order; clients match by id
Notifications within a batch produce no Response objects
A batch of only notifications returns nothing at all (not an empty array)
An empty array [] is a valid no-op

questions.explanation: All but E: an empty array is invalid and yields a single -32600 Invalid Request error response.

questions.question: Per the JSON-RPC 2.0 specification, which statements about notifications are true? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A notification is a Request object without an id member
The server MUST NOT reply to a notification — not even with an error
Notifications signal the sender's disinterest in any response
A request with id: null is a notification
All of the above

questions.explanation: Omitting id makes a notification; id: null is a (discouraged) regular request, kept distinct because v1 used null-id notifications.

questions.question: Which id-related rules does the JSON-RPC 2.0 spec state? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The id must be a String, a Number, or Null if present
Null as an id value is discouraged
Fractional number ids should be avoided because they may not round-trip exactly
The response id must equal the request id, or be Null when the request id couldn't be determined
All of the above

questions.explanation: Every clause is verbatim from §4 and §5 of the spec — a legitimate all-of-the-above.

questions.question: Which error codes carry their standard JSON-RPC meaning? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: -32700 Parse error
-32600 Invalid Request
-32601 Method not found
-32603 Internal error
All of the above

questions.explanation: The classic quartet (plus -32602 Invalid params) — all correct, so E is too.

questions.question: Which statements about method names and reserved space are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Method names beginning with 'rpc.' are reserved for rpc-internal methods and extensions
The error-code range -32768 to -32000 is reserved for pre-defined errors
MCP additionally reserves -32020 to -32099 for the specification, leaving -32000 to -32019 implementation-defined
Application servers may freely define a method named rpc.status
All of the above

questions.explanation: rpc.-prefixed names are exactly what applications must NOT define; A–C are the correct layering of JSON-RPC and MCP reservations.
